results.summary: This project is a placeholder Wokwi design with no implemented functionality. The documentation states that it does not work yet and that testing is to be determined. It requires no external hardware. The design is notable only as an incomplete student exercise.

This design implements a 2-bit adder that takes two 2-bit numbers as inputs and produces a 2-bit sum. It is intended to be tested by setting all inputs and observing the outputs. External hardware needed includes buttons for inputs and LEDs for outputs. The documentation is minimal and does not provide detailed implementation or test results.

This circuit generates Morse code for the letters J and R using a 4-bit synchronous counter and logic gates. It can be tested by connecting a 7-segment display and using a button to select between J and R. External hardware required includes a button, a 7-segment display, and a clock. The design is a simple educational example of Morse code generation.

This project is described as a basic project with minimal documentation. It has three pins and the documentation states it is Aditya's init and a basic project. External hardware is listed as 'Need to fill in'. The design is too poorly documented to determine its function or purpose.

This project implements a full adder that takes two 1-bit inputs X and Y plus a carry-in, and produces a sum and carry-out. It is tested by checking that the sum of X and Y equals the output sum. No external hardware is mentioned. The documentation is brief and does not include silicon test results.

This design is a 2-bit full adder that adds two numbers. It is tested by applying two input signals and observing the outputs. The documentation mentions external hardware but does not specify any. The project lacks detailed implementation notes and test results.

This project is titled 'gta6' and involves guessing a pin that lights an LED. It is tested by picking a pin and seeing if it lights up. No external hardware is required. The documentation is extremely sparse and does not describe any actual game functionality.

This design uses a 3-bit clock divider to spell a name by displaying a counter on a 7-segment display. It is tested by connecting a 7-segment display and a reset button, and observing the counter increment and reset. External hardware includes a 7-segment display and a reset button. The project is a simple educational example of sequential logic.

This design generates a VGA signal that displays 1D elementary cellular automata. It is used by plugging it into a VGA PMOD and a display. External hardware required is a VGA PMOD. The project is notable for its creative visual output and is implemented in Verilog.

This design recreates the Crossy Road game on an ASIC, where a chicken crosses roads while avoiding cars. It is controlled by a move button and outputs VGA video to a display. External hardware needed includes a debounced button and a 25 MHz clock. The project is notable for being a complete game implementation in Verilog.
